```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7.2, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 144, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
library(idiographic)
data(srl)
analysis_data <- subset(srl, name %in% c("Aisha", "Alice", "Anika", "Astrid", "Bjorn", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana", "Erik", "Eve", "Fatima", "Frank"))
```

Person-specific analysis rests on the properties of each individual time
series. Four descriptive functions are presented here. They are intended to
precede model fitting, because the amount of data, the variability of each
series, and the balance between stable and fluctuating variation determine
which models can be estimated and how their coefficients are interpreted.

| Question | Function |
|:--|:--|
| Is each person's series long and variable enough for analysis? | `describe_persons()` |
| Which variables co-vary within each person? | `correlate_persons()` |
| What share of the variance reflects stable differences between persons? | `variance_components()` |
| Do correlations computed across persons describe the correlations within persons? | `correlate_levels()` |

All examples use 12 learners from the bundled `srl` data set, each of whom
completed the same self-report items once a day, yielding 154 to 156
observations per learner.

## `describe_persons()`

### Purpose

`describe_persons()` returns a tidy data frame with one row for each
combination of learner and variable. Two learners measured on two variables
therefore yield four rows (Aisha's efficacy, Aisha's effort, Alice's efficacy,
Alice's effort). The columns describe the series in each row:

- **amount of data**: the number of observations (`n`), the number of missing
  values (`missing`), the number of days covered (`span`), and the typical and
  longest interval between consecutive observations (`gap_median`,
  `gap_max`);
- **level**: the mean, median, minimum, and maximum;
- **variability**: the standard deviation (`sd`), the root mean square
  successive difference (`rmssd`), and the lag-1 autocorrelation (`autocor`).

The two measures capture distinct properties of a series. The standard
deviation (SD) quantifies the spread of observations around the person's own
mean across the full observation period. The root mean square successive
difference (RMSSD) quantifies the magnitude of change between consecutive
occasions. A series that drifts slowly across a wide range and a series that
alternates sharply from day to day may have the same SD; the RMSSD separates
the two [@jahng2008]. The two quantities are related through the lag-1
autocorrelation $\rho_1$: for a stationary series,
$\text{RMSSD} \approx \text{SD}\sqrt{2(1-\rho_1)}$.

### Example

```{r description-table}
describe_persons(analysis_data, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "effort"), time = "day", subject = c("Aisha", "Alice"))
```

Both learners contributed 156 observations with no missing values. Mean
efficacy was 57 for Aisha and 36 for Alice, whereas the SDs (21 for both) and
the RMSSDs (27 and 29) were similar. The two learners therefore differed in
their typical level of efficacy and showed comparable variability.

The `time` argument defines the chronological order of observations within
each person; successive differences and autocorrelations are computed in that
order. Additional columns (floor and ceiling proportions, skewness, kurtosis,
linear trend, and the longest run of identical values) are returned with
`detail = "full"`.

### Visualisation

`plot_descriptives()` displays the SD on the horizontal axis and the RMSSD on
the vertical axis, with one point per person and variable.

```{r description-plot, fig.cap="Figure 1. Spread (SD) against day-to-day change (RMSSD) for efficacy and effort in 12 learners."}
descriptives <- describe_persons(analysis_data, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "effort"), time = "day")
plot_descriptives(descriptives)
```

The points lie close to a straight line, with RMSSD between 1.3 and 1.5 times
the SD. Under the relation given above, this ratio corresponds to small lag-1
autocorrelations: consecutive responses carried over little from one day to
the next. Strong carry-over would place points well below this line.

The figure also identifies atypical learners. Erik and Eve showed the largest
spread and the largest day-to-day change on both variables. Diana, Bob, and
Frank showed the least variability in efficacy, while Frank's effort was among
the most variable. Stability on one variable is therefore no indication of
stability on another.

### Assumptions and limitations

Successive differences and autocorrelations are meaningful only when rows are
ordered chronologically, so the `time` argument is required whenever the
stored row order differs from the order of measurement. Missing occasions
reduce the number of consecutive pairs available for the RMSSD and the
autocorrelation. A variable that is constant within a person has an undefined
correlation with any other variable and cannot serve as a predictor in that
person's model. The `trend` column describes a linear trend and is
insensitive to abrupt shifts or other non-linear change.

## `correlate_persons()`

### Purpose

`correlate_persons()` estimates, separately for each person, the Pearson
correlation between every pair of variables, together with a 95% confidence
interval obtained through Fisher's $z$ transformation. A positive
within-person correlation indicates that on occasions when one variable is
above that person's typical level, the other variable also tends to be above
its typical level.

### Example

```{r correlation-table}
correlations <- correlate_persons(analysis_data, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"), time = "day", subject = c("Aisha", "Alice"))
correlations
```

For Aisha, all three pairs were positively correlated, with coefficients
between 0.28 and 0.39. For Alice, efficacy and effort were positively
correlated (0.49), whereas monitoring was negatively correlated with both
efficacy (-0.23) and effort (-0.35). A single correlation computed across all
learners would conceal this difference in the direction of association.

### Visualisation

```{r correlation-plot, fig.cap="Figure 2. Within-person correlations with 95% confidence intervals for two learners."}
plot_correlations(correlations)
```

Each row corresponds to one person and one pair of variables, and rows are
ordered by the size of the correlation. All six confidence intervals exclude
zero.

### Assumptions and limitations

The coefficients describe association between variables measured on the
same occasion. Temporal precedence is examined with `fit_lm()` using lagged
predictors or with the dynamic network models. Each coefficient
is a bivariate association and is unadjusted for the remaining variables.
Because consecutive daily observations are serially dependent, the confidence
intervals may be too narrow. The `min_n` argument sets the minimum number of
complete pairs required for a coefficient to be reported, and constant
variables yield missing coefficients.

## `variance_components()`

### Purpose

`variance_components()` partitions the total variance of each variable into
a between-person component, reflecting differences in person means, and a
within-person component, reflecting fluctuation around each person's mean.
The intraclass correlation (ICC) is the between-person share of the total
variance. Values near 0 indicate that persons have similar means and that
variation arises mainly over time; values near 1 indicate stable differences
between persons with little fluctuation within them.

### Example

```{r variance-table}
components <- variance_components(analysis_data, vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"), id = "name")
components
```

The ICCs were 0.40 for efficacy, 0.38 for monitoring, and 0.26 for effort.
Between 60% and 74% of the variance of each variable was therefore located
within learners. The between-person component was nonetheless substantial.
Under these conditions a regression on the raw scores combines two distinct
associations: the association between a learner's daily deviations, and the
association between learners' average levels. `fit_within_between()`
estimates the two separately.

### Visualisation

```{r variance-plot, fig.cap="Figure 3. Between-person and within-person shares of variance."}
plot_variance(components)
```

### Assumptions and limitations

The reliability column refers to the precision of each person's mean and is
distinct from the reliability of a single occasion. A variable that is
constant within persons supports only between-person comparisons, and a
variable with no between-person variation supports only within-person
analysis.

## `correlate_levels()`

### Purpose

A correlation computed across persons is frequently used to describe how two
variables are related within each person. Fisher, Medaglia, and Jeronimus
[-@fisher2018] proposed a direct test of this generalization. Two
distributions of correlations are compared for the same pair of variables:

- **within persons**: one correlation per person, computed across that
  person's occasions;
- **between persons**: one correlation per occasion, computed across persons.
  The first observations of all persons form one cross-sectional data set,
  the second observations form a second one, and so on.

When group-level results generalize to individuals, the two distributions
have similar means and similar spreads. Fisher and colleagues found the
within-person standard deviation to be two to four times larger than the
between-person standard deviation across six samples.

### Example

This example uses all 36 learners in `srl`, so that every between-person
correlation is based on 36 persons and every within-person correlation on up
to 156 occasions.

```{r levels-table}
levels_result <- correlate_levels(srl, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"), time = "day")
levels_result
```

For efficacy and monitoring, and for monitoring and effort, the mean
correlations at the two levels were close (0.27 and 0.29; 0.25 and 0.28). For
efficacy and effort, the mean within-person correlation (0.36) was lower than
the mean between-person correlation (0.50). For all three pairs, the
within-person correlations were considerably more dispersed: their standard
deviation was 1.8 to 2.3 times that of the between-person correlations. For two of the three pairs, the correlation estimated across learners
therefore approximated the average within-learner correlation, while the
correlations of individual learners were distributed about twice as widely
around that value as the between-person correlations.

### Visualisation

`plot_levels()` displays the two distributions as density curves, following
the comparison of Fisher and colleagues. Densities place the 36
within-person and 156 between-person correlations on a common scale. The
ticks below each curve mark the correlations of the individual learners, and
the vertical stems mark the means.

```{r levels-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Figure 4. Distributions of within-person correlations (one per learner, solid) and between-person correlations (one per occasion, dashed) for three pairs of variables."}
plot_levels(levels_result)
```

### Temporal dependence

Serial dependence within persons can inflate the spread of within-person
correlations. With `lag_adjust = TRUE`, each variable is first regressed on
its own lag-1 value and on the lag-1 value of the other variable, and the
within-person correlations are computed from the residuals.

```{r levels-lag}
summary(correlate_levels(srl, id = "name", vars = c("efficacy", "monitoring", "effort"), time = "day", lag_adjust = TRUE))
```

The adjustment left the results essentially unchanged: the mean
within-person correlations changed by at most 0.003, and the ratios of
standard deviations remained between 1.8 and 2.3. This agrees with the small
lag-1 autocorrelations implied by Figure 1. The larger spread of
within-person correlations is therefore attributable to differences between
learners in how the variables co-vary.

### Assumptions and limitations

The between-person correlations require occasions that are comparable across
persons; here the $t$-th observation of every learner is treated as one
occasion. With fewer persons than occasions, each between-person correlation
rests on a small sample, and its sampling error contributes to the
between-person spread. The ratio of standard deviations is a descriptive
index and is reported without a significance test.

## Choice among the four functions

`describe_persons()` is applied first, to establish that every person has
sufficient observations and variation. `variance_components()` then indicates
whether variation is located mainly between or within persons, which
determines whether the two levels must be separated in subsequent models.
`correlate_persons()` provides an initial account of within-person
co-variation, and `correlate_levels()` indicates how well correlations
estimated across persons describe the correlations within them.

The four functions are descriptive. Models are fitted with `fit_lm()` for a
single outcome and several predictors, with `fit_within_between()` for
separate within-person and between-person effects, and with `pool_coefs()`
for summarising the heterogeneity of person-specific effects.
